The next number is **21**.

This is the **Fibonacci sequence**, one of the most famous patterns in mathematics. Each number is the sum of the two numbers before it:

- 1 + 1 = 2
- 1 + 2 = 3
- 2 + 3 = 5
- 3 + 5 = 8
- 5 + 8 = 13
- **8 + 13 = 21**

Written as a rule, if F(n) is the nth term, then F(n) = F(n−1) + F(n−2), starting with F(1) = 1 and F(2) = 1. Continuing the pattern gives 34, 55, 89, 144, 233, and so on.

### Where it comes from

The sequence is named after Leonardo of Pisa, known as Fibonacci, who introduced it to European readers in his 1202 book *Liber Abaci*. He used it to solve a puzzle about rabbit populations: if each pair of rabbits produces a new pair every month starting from their second month, how many pairs will there be after a year? The answer follows exactly this sequence. Indian mathematicians had described the same numbers centuries earlier while studying patterns in Sanskrit poetry.

### Why it's interesting

**The golden ratio.** If you divide each Fibonacci number by the one before it, the results get closer and closer to about 1.618, known as the golden ratio (φ). For example, 21 ÷ 13 ≈ 1.615 and 144 ÷ 89 ≈ 1.618.

**Nature.** Fibonacci numbers show up surprisingly often in living things. The number of petals on many flowers (3, 5, 8, 13), the spirals in sunflower heads and pinecones, and the arrangement of leaves around a stem often match Fibonacci numbers. This happens because these arrangements pack seeds or leaves efficiently.

**Computer science.** The sequence is a classic example for teaching recursion and dynamic programming, and it appears in algorithms such as Fibonacci search and Fibonacci heaps.

### A quick caution

Strictly speaking, any finite list of numbers can be continued in more than one way if you invent a complicated enough rule. But in a question like this, the Fibonacci pattern is clearly the intended one, and 21 is the answer you'd be expected to give.

Zebras are famous for their black and white stripes, and scientists have wondered for a long time why they have them. There are a few ideas, but the strongest one is a bit surprising: the stripes help keep biting flies away!

**The fly problem**

In Africa, where zebras live, there are lots of flies that bite animals to drink their blood. Two of the worst are horseflies and tsetse flies. These bites hurt, and they can also spread diseases that make animals very sick. So for a zebra, keeping flies away is really important.

**How stripes confuse flies**

Scientists did a fun experiment. They put coats on horses, some plain and some with black and white stripes, and watched what the flies did. The flies flew toward the striped horses but had trouble landing on them. Many of them flew right past or bumped into them instead of landing smoothly!

Why? Flies have eyes that are very different from ours. When they get close, the stripes seem to mess up how they see movement and distance. It's a bit like trying to land on something while the ground looks like it is flickering. The fly gets confused and can't slow down properly, so it misses.

Tsetse flies also seem to dislike landing on striped surfaces, so stripes may help zebras avoid these dangerous flies too.

**Other ideas**

Some scientists think stripes might also help zebras stay a little cooler in the hot sun, or help them recognize each other, because every zebra's stripes are different, like a fingerprint.

But the fly idea has the most evidence. So a zebra's stripes are a bit like a built-in bug spray!

We study the effective geometry of noncommutative branes arising as solutions of Yang-Mills matrix models of the IKKT type. Fluctuations of the matrices around a background brane are shown to propagate on an effective metric determined by the embedding and the underlying Poisson structure, rather than the induced metric alone. Using heat kernel techniques adapted to the matrix setting, we compute the one-loop effective action for scalar, gauge and fermionic fluctuations in the semi-classical limit. In the maximally supersymmetric model the leading divergences cancel, while the remaining contributions induce gravitational terms, including an Einstein-Hilbert action, for the effective metric. We discuss the implications for emergent gravity and the conditions under which the resulting dynamics are compatible with four-dimensional general relativity.

Globular cluster (GC) systems in a wide range of galaxies display broad, frequently bimodal metallicity distributions, and the origin of this structure remains a central question in models of galaxy assembly. We present a homogeneous analysis of GC metallicity distributions for a sample of early- and late-type galaxies spanning roughly three orders of magnitude in host stellar mass, using optical and near-infrared colors calibrated against spectroscopic metallicities. We fit the distributions with Gaussian mixture models and assess the statistical significance of multimodality in each system. Bimodality is common in massive galaxies but becomes less pronounced toward lower luminosities, where metal-poor clusters dominate. The mean metallicities of both the metal-poor and metal-rich subpopulations correlate with host galaxy luminosity, with the metal-rich relation being steeper. We compare these trends with predictions from hierarchical merging, in situ formation and accretion-driven scenarios, and find that the observed scaling relations favor a picture in which metal-poor GCs are largely accreted from low-mass satellites while metal-rich GCs form within the host during its main star-forming phase.

Not meaningfully. A banana's total calorie content stays roughly the same as it ripens, about 105 calories for a medium fruit. What changes is the form of the carbohydrates: as the banana ripens, enzymes convert starch into simple sugars like sucrose, glucose, and fructose, which is why it tastes sweeter.

There is one small nuance. Unripe bananas contain a lot of resistant starch, which your small intestine doesn't fully digest, so you absorb slightly fewer calories from a green banana than from a ripe one. Ripe bananas also raise blood sugar faster, but the difference in usable energy is modest.

Waking up refreshed is mostly decided the night before and in the first half hour after your alarm. A few things make the biggest difference:

**Before bed**
- **Keep a consistent schedule.** Going to sleep and waking up at the same time every day, including weekends, is the single most effective habit. Your body clock starts preparing you to wake before the alarm goes off.
- **Get enough sleep.** Most adults need 7–9 hours. No morning routine can make up for regularly sleeping five.
- **Cut caffeine after early afternoon** and go easy on alcohol, which knocks out the deeper stages of sleep even if it helps you doze off.
- **Dim screens and lights** for the last hour. Bright light late at night pushes your body clock later.
- **Keep the bedroom cool, dark, and quiet.** Around 18°C (65°F) suits most people.

**When you wake up**
- **Don't hit snooze.** Short bursts of broken sleep tend to leave you groggier. Put the alarm across the room if you need to.
- **Get light right away.** Open the curtains or step outside for a few minutes. Daylight is the strongest signal to your brain that the day has started.
- **Drink a glass of water.** You've gone hours without fluids, and mild dehydration adds to that sluggish feeling.
- **Move a little.** A few stretches, a short walk, or some light exercise gets blood flowing.
- **Wait a bit before coffee.** Some people find that holding off 30–60 minutes helps them avoid an afternoon crash, though the evidence is mixed. Try it and see.

**A useful trick:** sleep runs in roughly 90-minute cycles, and waking in the middle of deep sleep is what makes you feel foggy. If you count back in 90-minute blocks from your wake time (plus about 15 minutes to fall asleep), you're more likely to wake during lighter sleep. Sleep-tracking alarms that wake you within a time window work on the same idea.

If you're getting plenty of sleep and still wake up exhausted, it's worth checking with a doctor. Problems like sleep apnea, low iron, or thyroid issues are common and treatable.

The Scheveningen (pawns on e6 and d6 for Black in the Open Sicilian) is a flexible "small centre" setup, and White has several well-established ways to play against it. They fall into a few broad families.

## 1. The Keres Attack (6.g4)

After 1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5.Nc3 e6, the immediate **6.g4** is one of White's most aggressive and respected tries.

- **Idea:** Kick the f6-knight with g4–g5 before Black has castled, gaining space and disrupting Black's development.
- White typically follows up with h4, Rg1, Be3, Qd2 or Qe2, and long castling.
- Black often responds with ...h6 to slow down g5, or with ...Nc6/...a6 setups, accepting a sharp middlegame.

Because of the Keres, many Black players reach the Scheveningen via the Najdorf (5...a6 then ...e6) or the Taimanov/Paulsen move orders to sidestep it.

## 2. The English Attack (Be3, f3, Qd2, g4, O-O-O)

This is the main modern approach, especially against Najdorf-Scheveningen hybrids.

- **Setup:** Be3, f3, Qd2, castle queenside, then g4–g5 and h4–h5.
- **Idea:** Opposite-side castling leads to a pawn race. White storms the kingside while Black counterattacks on the queenside with ...b5–b4, ...Rc8, and pressure down the c-file.
- f3 supports g4 and prevents ...Ng4 hitting the e3-bishop.
- Key themes include Nd5 sacrifices, g5 to dislodge the f6-knight, and timing the pawn storm to arrive first.

## 3. The Classical Approach (Be2, O-O, f4)

The older, more positional system, associated with players like Karpov.

- **Typical moves:** Be2, O-O, f4, Kh1, a4, Be3, and often Qe1–g3 or Bf3.
- **a4** is an important prophylactic move, clamping down on Black's ...b5 expansion.
- **Plans for White:**
  - **e4–e5 break:** Opening the centre while Black's king is still in the middle or the d6-pawn is weak.
  - **f4–f5:** Pressuring e6, sometimes followed by fxe6 to open the f-file or gain the d5/f5 squares.
  - **g4–g5 kingside storm:** Even with kings on the same side, White can push g4–g5 to drive away the f6-knight, supported by Rf3–h3 or Qg3 ideas.
  - **Qe1–g3 or Qe1–h4:** Rerouting the queen to the kingside to put pressure on g7 and support a mating attack.

## 4. The Sozin/Velimirovic (Bc4)

When Black has played ...Nc6, White can aim the bishop at e6 with **Bc4**.

- **Velimirovic Attack:** Bc4, Be3, Qe2, O-O-O, followed by g4–g5 and sacrificial ideas like Nd5 or Nf5.
- The bishop on c4 (often retreating to b3) eyes e6 and supports sacrificial breakthroughs against Black's king.

## Recurring Themes Across All Systems

- **The d5 square:** Black often tries to keep White out of d5; White's Nd5 sacrifices are a constant tactical motif.
- **The e5 break:** When Black's pieces are passive, e4–e5 can open lines toward the king.
- **f4–f5 against e6:** Undermining the Scheveningen pawn chain.
- **Restricting ...b5:** Moves like a4 (in classical lines) slow Black's queenside play.
- **Fighting ...d5:** Black's freeing ...d6–d5 break, if achieved safely, usually equalises, so White aims to prevent or punish it.

In short, White chooses between an immediate kingside pawn storm (Keres or English Attack) and a slower buildup with f4, a4, and central or kingside breaks (Classical). The choice usually comes down to style and to the move order Black uses to reach the Scheveningen.

That vertical strip is a **security thread**, and it is one of the main features that makes a $20 bill hard to counterfeit.

**What it is**

The thread is a thin polymer strip set into the paper when the note is made. It is not printed on the surface. It sits inside the cotton-linen blend that US currency is printed on, so you can barely see it in normal light. Hold the bill up to a lamp or a window and it shows up as a dark line running from top to bottom.

On a $20, the thread is to the left of Andrew Jackson's portrait. If you look closely you'll see tiny printing on it that reads "USA TWENTY," along with a small flag. The text alternates direction, so you can read it from either side of the note.

**Why it's there**

Counterfeiters usually work with ordinary paper and a good printer or copier. A scanner can reproduce what's printed on the surface of a bill, but it can't reproduce something embedded inside the paper. A fake might have a line drawn or printed where the thread should be, but it will be visible without backlighting, it won't carry clear microprinting, and it won't react the way the real one does under ultraviolet light.

**The UV test**

Under a UV (black) light, the security thread on a genuine $20 glows green. Each denomination glows a different color: blue for the $5, orange for the $10, yellow for the $50, and pink for the $100. The placement also changes from bill to bill, which stops people from bleaching a $5 and reprinting it as a $100. The thread position and glow color would give it away.

**How it fits with other features**

The thread is designed to be checked alongside the other security features on the note:

- A **watermark** of Jackson, also visible when held to light, on the right side
- **Color-shifting ink** in the lower-right "20," which changes from copper to green when tilted
- **Microprinting** around the portrait and borders
- Raised, slightly rough-feeling ink from intaglio printing

Security threads were added to US paper money in the early 1990s, when high-quality color copiers became cheap enough to be a real threat. Since then they've become one of the quickest checks a cashier can make: hold the bill up to the light and look for the strip.

**Is Khamenei Following Khomeini's Path to a "Bitter Peace"?**

As Iran's negotiators press toward a nuclear agreement with world powers, a growing number of observers are asking whether Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei is preparing for his own version of a historic compromise, one with clear echoes of the decision his predecessor made more than a quarter-century ago.

In 1988, after eight years of devastating war with Iraq, Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, the founder of the Islamic Republic, agreed to a United Nations-brokered ceasefire with Saddam Hussein. For a leader who had vowed to fight until Saddam was toppled, it was a humiliating reversal. Khomeini famously told the nation that accepting the truce was "more deadly than drinking poison," but said he did so for the survival of the revolution. He died less than a year later.

Iranian journalist and author Nazila Fathi argues that Khamenei, now in his mid-70s and reportedly in uncertain health, may be weighing a similar calculation. Years of sanctions have battered Iran's economy, driven up inflation and fueled frustration among a young population eager for jobs and engagement with the outside world.

According to Fathi, Khamenei has long cast the United States as Iran's chief enemy and has publicly voiced deep skepticism about the talks. Yet he has also given President Hassan Rouhani and Foreign Minister Mohammad Javad Zarif room to negotiate, describing his approach as "heroic flexibility." Fathi suggests that this may reflect a leader trying to put the country on a more stable footing before his death, and to secure the future of the system he has guarded for more than 25 years.

The comparison has its limits. Khomeini ended a shooting war in which hundreds of thousands had died, while Khamenei faces economic pressure rather than battlefield defeat. Hardliners in Tehran continue to oppose concessions, and Khamenei has been careful to avoid any appearance of surrender.

Still, analysts say, the parallel is hard to ignore. If a deal is reached, Khamenei may find himself, like his predecessor, accepting a compromise he once rejected, and hoping history judges it as the choice that saved the Islamic Republic.

Money and Happiness

Many people believe that if they have a lot of money, they will be happy forever. Other people say money cannot buy happiness. In my opinion, money is important for a happy life, but it is not the key. I think it is only one part of the picture.

First, I want to say that money is necessary. We need money for food, a house, clothes and to go to the doctor. If a family don't have enough money, they worry every day and it is very hard to feel happy. My uncle lost his job two years ago, and I saw how stressed he was. He could not sleep well and he was angry a lot. When he found a new job, he became more relax and smiled again. So I agree that money can take away many problems.

However, after we have enough money for basic things, more money does not make us much more happier. For example, some famous people are very rich, but they are lonely or they have problems with drugs. I read on the internet that many lottery winners are not happier after some years. Some of them even lose all their money and their friends. This shows that money alone is not enough.

In my experience, the things that make me most happy are free or very cheap. When I spend time with my family at dinner, when I laugh with my friends after school, or when I play football in the park, I feel really good. Nobody can buy these moments in a shop. Also, helping other people make me feel happy. Last year I helped my neighbor to carry her shopping every week, and she always thanked me with a big smile. I did not get money for it, but I felt very warm inside.

Another important thing is health. If you are very rich but you are sick all the time, you cannot enjoy your life. Money can pay for a good hospital, but it cannot always give you back your health.

In conclusion, I think money is important because it gives us safety and help us to live without big worries. But real happiness come from people we love, good health and doing things that have meaning. So money is helpful, but it is not the key to happiness. If I have to choose, I prefer to have a normal salary and a happy family than to be rich and alone.
